utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. For the record, all the accused are here. Representation is as yesterday, minus Mr. Haynes for the Pandurevic team. Will he be coming later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But nothing serious; in other words, no problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIS
utterances.text: No, he's fit and well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Incidentally, two days ago we had raised some housekeeping matters. Only left over was the Zivanovic -- or the Popovic two outstanding motions, which I understand you have no objection to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So those two motions, Mr. Zivanovic, are granted -- are being granted now orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Yesterday, I discussed at some length the uncertainties hanging over the sequence of events at Kravica warehouse on the afternoon and evening of 13 July. I now turn to address you more briefly on the uncertainties as to who was there during that time-period, and in particular the Prosecution's allegation that some of Borovcanin's subordinates were: A, there, and, B, taking part in the killings. Now, the Prosecution asserts in their brief, at paragraph 1938, that: "No VRS troops were deployed to the road" on 12 July. And then at paragraph 1950 of their brief, they say: "The evidence in the case establishes that Borovcanin's MUP forces were present and in control of the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road from Kravica village to Hrncici on 12 July and then during all of 13 July. No VRS troops were deployed to the road at this time." Now, the Prosecution has no direct evidence substantiating that any of Borovcanin's men participated in either killing event, so the absence of other units in the area is a critical circumstantial indicator on which they rely to argue that the escorting between Sandici Meadow and Kravica warehouse, and then the guarding at the warehouse, and then subsequently the killing of the prisoners at the warehouse, must have been done by Borovcanin's men. We did hear the Prosecutor qualifying that claim last Friday, so I don't know to what extent they actually still maintain that there were no VRS forces in the area. But coming up on the screen now on e-court in front of you is a graphic representation of just some of the evidence in this case showing how very incorrect that claim is, and we document that evidence in our brief at paragraphs 132, 168, 169, and 185. Many witnesses, including Muslim witnesses with no motive to lie at all, as well as documents and intercepts, indicate that VRS soldiers were active in significant numbers along the road on the 13th of July. In fact, the evidence shows that they were right there on the critical segment of road between Kravica village and Hrncici, including, most importantly of all, men from two units of the Bratunac Brigade at the Kravica warehouse itself. And it's not just one man, as the Prosecution has said during its closing remarks; it's eight men, some of whom held command positions in their units. The inference that I think you can reasonably draw is that there were a lot more than just eight men from the Bratunac Brigade in the warehouse compound at that time. The Prosecution tries to claim, in its brief at paragraph 1997, that Borovcanin admitted during his interview that a group of 30 members of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment were present at the warehouse when he arrived, when he passed by along the road. They accomplish this by an extraordinary misrepresentation of Borovcanin's words, stitching together an answer about people having witnessed Mladic's speech at Sandici Meadow at page 72 of the March interview, Borovcanin interview, with a totally separate passage describing who he saw on the road in front of the warehouse, which is at page 64 of his March interview. I simply invite Your Honours to read those passages carefully, and you'll see that the assertion made by the Prosecution is untenable. Now, I said there was no direct evidence of Borovcanin's men participating in the killings. There is direct evidence, however, from Witness 111 on this issue. And 111 says that the men guarding him at the warehouse were not the same men as had been guarding him at the meadow. That's what he says in no uncertain terms. Now, Your Honours, we say a great deal more in our brief about these issues, and so I simply commend those sections to your attention. It's not just the evidence about who's there; it's also the evidence about the escorting. In other words, how do those prisoners get from Sandici Meadow down to Kravica warehouse? I suggest to you that that's an important issue for the subsequent inference of who is at the warehouse. And, incredibly, given the circumstantial nature of the Prosecution case, there's virtually no discussion of those issues. And I think that's an important deficiency in a case that's based on the assertion that Borovcanin's men simply must have been there. One comment on this circumstantial nature of the case. The Prosecution complained that we were unfair, in our brief, to suggest that this was a circumstantial case by choice, not by necessity. And I heard the Prosecution excusing their decision or explaining their decision not to subpoena these two particular witnesses because that would not have been allowed in the home jurisdictions of some of the prosecutors on this team. But that may be so, Your Honours, but it's not very relevant. They could have compelled these individuals, but they didn't do so, and that does amount to a choice, however that choice came about. And, more broadly, it's not just these two witnesses. Now, Your Honours, let's assume, notwithstanding all of the very serious doubts about the sequence of events at Kravica warehouse in relation to the timing of Borovcanin passing by, let's say notwithstanding all of those question marks and doubts that I say must be there in your minds, let's say that you reach a factual finding that he did know that there may have been criminal acts going on, but then you find that there's no basis, no credible basis, no sufficient basis to find that his subordinates are there. I suggest, Your Honours, that this would bring you to the issue of omission liability. The Prosecution is arguing in its brief that even if the perpetrators were not subordinates, that Borovcanin had a duty to enter the warehouse because he had men nearby, and he should have gone in there, if necessary, with guns blazing to quell the shooting. Now, we've addressed this argument at length, the legal foundations of this claim, from paragraphs 357 to 382 of our brief. The issue of omission liability for the actions of non-subordinates is a complicated legal issue. It's a critical and important legal issue. Despite all the confusions, one thing that is clear, whether you take the Blaskic standard or the Mrksic standard, is that a pre-condition of this form of liability is custody of the prisoners. It's an amazing omission from the Prosecution case and brief that nowhere do they define custody. We do. We give you a definition of custody, and I can tell you that the facts don't come close to establishing that those men were in Borovcanin's custody. And on that point, again, I commend you to our brief. I move now to my third topic overall in my remarks, and that is the reliability of the Prosecution brief. Aside from the misrepresentations and incompleteness of the analysis that I've already discussed, it brims with previously unheard of allegations. There are far many to go through in detail, but I'm going to go through a few signal examples, and I'm going to add one example of what I say is a rather serious misstatement of evidence. At paragraph 606 of the Prosecution brief, which is coming up in front of you on the screen, on the left-hand side of your screen, you see a description of the audio -- of a portion of audio from the trial video. Now, as you know, there are transcripts of this audio in evidence. In fact, there are two transcripts of this audio, one transcript associated with the Petrovic footage and one transcript associated with the trial video. Now, one would have thought that given the procedures of admission of transcripts and the ability for both parties then to ask questions to witnesses on the basis of those transcripts, that in a final brief they'd use one of those admitted transcripts. Now, I don't have any problem, frankly, with the Prosecution, in a final brief, interpreting the audio in their own way, and I'm not exactly sure why they've done what they've done in paragraph 606 of their brief, but what you see here is that they've made their own -- they've given their own interpretations. And, again, I don't mind that, but you'd think that this would warrant a mention at least in the footnote, saying, This is what we're doing. Second example. The Prosecution tries to add three units to Mr. Borovcanin's command, the 2nd Deserters Company and the 2nd and 5th Zvornik PJP Companies, and this is at footnote 408 and paragraphs 1939 and 1944, amongst other references. Let's go to paragraph 18 of the indictment. It says: "Note: MUP units acting under the command and control of Ljubomir Borovcanin are explicitly identified as doing so in the paragraphs below." That paragraph was inserted following your order which said the Prosecution is ordered to amend the indictment as follows: "... to plead expressly Ljubomir Borovcanin's command and control over MUP forces -- the MUP forces performing alleged acts from 12 to 17 July 1995 throughout the relevant time ..." Despite these instructions, you'll see no mention of any of these three units in the indictment. You'll see no mention of any of these three units in the pre-trial brief. And when you, Mr. President, asked the Prosecutor on Friday to state whether the Prosecution had or had not, during its case, made this allegation, you didn't get an answer. You got an argument about the merits, and that speaks volumes. Let me give you one example of the OTP's position about just one of these units while they were questioning their own expert. After a series of objections from other Defence teams about the nature of the testimony that was being elicited, Mr. Butler finally answers or gives an answer to a series of questions and says: "The 2nd Company" of the Zvornik CJB - I'm inserting that because that's what he's referring to - "is not designated as being directly under the command of Colonel Borovcanin." Then the Prosecutor says, and this is at page 19832 of the transcript: "Thank you. Perhaps we could take a break, Your Honour. I mean, for me to have to go through that to get a piece of exculpatory information for Borovcanin is beyond me." Well, apparently it wasn't exculpatory enough to prevent the Prosecution from arguing the contrary in its closing brief. And aside from being improper, the claim is wrong, as is discussed in section 2 of our brief concerning the parallel chains of MUP command that were in operation at that time in that area. Now, what's the prejudice of this claim? It seems innocuous enough, but adding the 2nd Deserters Unit to Mr. Borovcanin's portfolio is significant to one claim made by the OTP, and that is that Borovcanin's men were somehow involved in the clean-up operation at Kravica warehouse on the 14th of July. There's absolutely no evidence to support that, with one exception, and that is PW-170's uncorroborated testimony. And, remember, there were two other witnesses there that day, as discussed in our brief. Your Honours, just to reassure you, what you're seeing on your screen is not being publicly broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I think I settled that yesterday with the Registrar, and in agreement, of course, after consultation with my colleagues, so you don't have to worry about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. PW-170's uncorroborated testimony that he saw what he refers to as Jahorinci, that he sees Jahorinci there on the 14th of July. So the expanded allegation -- the inclusion of the 2nd Deserters Company now allows them to overcome PW-170's failure to give any more specific identification as to who was there. So by what seems to be a marginal and harmless or at least innocuous expansion of its case, they get to tick off one or more -- one of those boxes that they listed in their check-list at the beginning. It's a significant factual allegation being made through the back door. And, Your Honours, if the Prosecution wants to allege de facto command over these units, that's fine, but there are factual issues associated with such a claim, and that has to be established through evidence at trial, and we have to know that that's what they're claiming. And we have to have a chance to respond, other than getting up during closing arguments and responding to it, based essentially on hypothetical assertions. And, again, that's particularly true where we all know that there were two parallel chains of command in operation at that time in that place. Now, I suggest that there is a need to be on guard against the insidious prejudice of these kinds of claims. And, incidentally, as to the issue of responsibility for burials on 14 July, we stand by everything that we say in paragraph 201 of our brief as to who was directing and performing that process, and it wasn't Borovcanin or his men. Third example. At paragraph 1865 of the Prosecution brief is the previously unheard of claim that the 2nd Sekovici Detachment and the 1st PJP Company are still present along the road on 14 July. Again, another claim not found in the indictment, despite the clear instructions in the indictment. This proposition was never put to any witness. It's not found in the pre-trial brief. It wasn't in the opening statement. It wasn't in any other of the accepted mechanisms by which you communicate your case. And, in any event, there isn't one wit of evidence to support it. Fourth example. In discussing the alleged responsibility of Borovcanin for forcible transfer, the Prosecutor, at paragraph 1911 of its brief, mentions Momir Nikolic's role in Potocari on 12 and 13 July, and this mention is only brief and passing. In other words, in the Borovcanin section of the brief, it's as if Momir Nikolic has no role whatsoever. When you flip to the Popovic section of the brief, however, you find a very different story. At paragraph 2377, after a listing of the units that were present there, you see the assertion: "Coordinating the action of the disparate Serb forces deployed in Potocari was necessary to carry out the planned operation." We entirely agree with that statement. The OTP brief goes on in the next paragraph, 2378, with apparent approval, that: "Momir Nikolic testified that he thus oversaw the engagement of the military police and the 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade who were directly involved in these activities, and advised Dusko Jevic of the MUP Special Brigade, which was similarly involved." Well, two observations here, Your Honours. First, how is it possible that Nikolic is overseeing two units engaged in this task, but only offering advice to the third? There's no explanation given for this distinction. Nikolic was overseeing all units involved in the task, and it wasn't merely based on his position as the security officer of the Bratunac Brigade, but because he was told to do so and invested with the authority to do so by Mladic and Radoslav Jankovic, both of whom were right there on the scene at the time. It's just that simple, and that is what is recognised at 2378. And we submit that there's no foundation for saying that he was, on the one hand, overseeing these two units, but merely giving advice to Dusko Jevic, on the other hand. I think the words of Lord Justice Ward of the English Court of Appeal are apposite here: "Riding two horses at the same time is always difficult enough. Riding them when they are charging in opposite directions is an altogether remarkable feat." The Prosecution makes a previously unstated perfidy allegation against Borovcanin and asserts at paragraph 1973 that: "Momir Nikolic would only have undertaken to drive along the road in an UNPROFOR vehicle and call prisoners down if Borovcanin had ordered or agreed to this tactic." Now, first of all, Borovcanin said in his interview that he was only present along the road first early in the morning on the 13th and then again at around 4.00 p.m. The Prosecution never suggested otherwise, they called no evidence suggesting otherwise, and Nikolic, on the other hand, starts driving up and down the road in his APC in the early afternoon. And we discussed the references to this testimony in our brief at paragraphs 173 to 174. So how could Borovcanin have ordered and agreed to a tactic if he wasn't even there? And second, perhaps more importantly, the claim that Borovcanin would have had the authority to issue orders to Momir Nikolic is another completely unprecedented allegation, and in fact it's contradicted by their own expert's testimony at 20458 of the transcript of this case. And, third, the perfidy claim is flatly contradicted by the trial video at two hours and thirty-eight minutes, where you can see one of Borovcanin's men telling a Muslim prisoner to shout to his colleagues in the forest and say that he is with the Serbs. That's not perfidy. Your Honours, these are just five examples of erroneous statements of evidence or case expansions. There are more, many more, but I leave it to Your Honours to be alert to these misstatements. I suggest to you that, unfortunately, this is a brief which requires you to be alert to these misstatements. And three brief remarks about the credibility of Borovcanin's interview. First, the Prosecution claims that Borovcanin lied in his interview because he said he was ordered to go to Zvornik instead of having said, as he should have apparently said, that he was told to go towards Zvornik. This argument might have had some validity if Borovcanin had then gone on in his interview to deny where his men were; namely, along the critical piece of road on 12 and 13 July. But that's not what he did. He honestly and accurately described exactly where his units were deployed, as the evidence in this case has confirmed. So I suggest to you that this, essentially, is just unreasonable nitpicking. And, in fact, we went back and checked the B/C/S transcript and found out that on at least two occasions during this exchange, the words used, as translated, were "towards," not "to." Second, Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Sorry to interrupt you, but I think on this particular point that you raise now, that you mention now, if you are specific as to the exact page and line, et cetera, because having heard you, I think we will need to have the official translators look into it, the original interview in the original language, and find out exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe I do have the correct reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you pass it on, later on, to your colleague -- other colleagues, and to the Registrar, I will look after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I certainly will. Thank you, Your Honour. Second, Milan Lukic. The Prosecution uses an intercept, and that's the only evidence in the case on this issue showing that a bus, containing some of Lukic's men, had broken down on the way to Srebrenica. But that doesn't show, Your Honours, that Lukic, himself, wasn't there or that at least some of his men showed up with him. And, indeed, Your Honours, I suggest to you that evidence that there was at least one bus heading to Srebrenica actually suggests to you that Lukic was there and that he may have had other men with him. So this great example of Borovcanin's untruthfulness is baseless. Third, the Prosecution argues that Borovcanin was inconsistent about his re-subordination to the VRS. Borovcanin did re-affirm repeatedly that the consequence of Order 6495 was that he was re-subordinated to the VRS. Now, it is true, Your Honours, that there is one passage where he denies that, in the context of some questions relating to General Krstic. Now, there are two responses to this. First, it's not unreasonable to believe that an interviewee could make a mistake at the end of three days of fairly hostile questioning. You don't reasonably have to conclude that he's got -- that he is intending to mislead, and you certainly -- that certainly doesn't lead to the inference that he's trying to cover up some kind of criminal motive. And, second, and related to this possibility of a mistake, and as you know from having read section 2 of our brief and having heard our expert, Professor Ristivojevic, the precise modalities of re-subordination are not necessarily without subtlety. And I suggest simply to you that based on that complexity, the complexity of the legislation, and the complexity of the situation on the ground at that time, that what he was saying is what he might well have actually believed when he was answering those questions. Now, one point on the forcible transfer allegation against Mr. Borovcanin, which is otherwise discussed at great length in our brief, and I would say only this: Military men do need bright-line rules when they go into combat in order for IHL to have any real applicability in those circumstances. The Srebrenica enclave had been a notorious source of attacks on Serb forces for years. Those attacks were specifically designed, as the Prosecution has admitted, to pull Serb forces away from other fronts. So when a commander, who is 150, 200 kilometres away, receives an order to come to that front and engage in combat with Muslim forces, he has to be able to rely on the good-faith belief that the operation -- that the intention -- that the purpose of the operation is actually to combat those military forces, and that's why Article 32 of the ICC Statute says that orders need only be disobeyed -- that you only need to stand down, in the words of the Prosecution, if those orders are manifestly unlawful. And the bottom line is that in those circumstances, engaging in the military campaign against the Srebrenica enclave was not manifestly unlawful. Her Honour Judge Prost asked my colleague yesterday whether wholesale detentions, such as those occurred in Srebrenica, were lawful under IHL. Now, Your Honours, I would direct you first and foremost to section 7(3) of our brief, where we discuss in detail the applicable provisions and the state practice, more importantly, that supports this claim, and I suggest to you you can be reassured about the correctness of what's stated in that section because the Prosecution, if you look carefully at their pleadings, have never suggested that the detentions, per se, were unlawful. The claim is either that the manner of detentions were abusive and improper or, B, that there was a hidden agenda which was criminal. That's the way they've pleaded their case, and I suggest to you that that's why there is no claim, no allegation, no count in the indictment of unlawful confinement, which they could have charged under IHL if that is what had happened. Now, having said what I just said, this is a fact-dependent inquiry, no doubt about it, but the critical factor here is not only the circumstances about conscription, combatants wearing civilian clothing, the presence of an armed column nearby, testimony that there were armed Muslim forces in and around Potocari on the 11th and even, according to one UNPROFOR witness, on the 13th. Those are all circumstances that go into this analysis, but perhaps the most important aspect of the analysis is the duration of the detention. No doubt, it would be improper to detain a huge number of people like this over a long period of time without any scrutiny or status determination. That would be improper, no doubt. But over a period of 24 hours, 48 hours, 72 hours, in the context that I've just described to you, yes, that is lawful, that is allowed, that is appropriate, and it's what other Western militaries have done in the past. Your Honours, I come back, in conclusion, to the standard that applies in a circumstantial case. The Prosecution must establish that their scenario is the only reasonable interpretation based on the fragments of evidence that they've presented to you. We have only to show you or even suggest to you that any one of a number of other possible scenarios is not unreasonable. The Prosecution case does not come close. That's not because of any negligence on their part. This is a brilliant and tough Prosecution team, but their circumstantial case against Mr. Borovcanin is incoherent, inconsistent, and fundamentally untrustworthy. Your Honours, the burden falls now to you to assess the evidence, to consider the law. I humbly invite you to read our brief with a fine-toothed comb. I suggest that when you evaluate the big picture and the smaller pictures, and all the pictures in between, you'll see at the end of the day that the Prosecution case is little more than speculation, speculation that isn't even very plausible. They've not proven their case beyond a reasonable doubt. They've not proven that Borovcanin was involved in a mass murder plot, and they've not proven that he was involved in a forcible transfer operation. I thank you for your patience, Your Honours. And if you have any questions, I'll do my best to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Stole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Clearly, what law is relevant and applicable depends on the facts, such as the Trial Chamber, at the end of the day, will establish this to be beyond reasonable doubt, and clearly the Defence has to state its position on the facts and the law under various alternatives, as indeed you have done, Mr. Gosnell, and perhaps even more so in cases where there may be a development as to which possible relevant facts alleged by the Prosecution. And I think I've been able to follow and understand your submissions. On one point, though, I would like to make sure that I have understood you well, and that is with reference to the final brief. On page 190, you discuss forms of criminal responsibility alleged, and the first there is superior responsibility under Article 7(3). So that is the context of the paragraph I'm taking you to. On page 195, on top of that page, you have this -- immediately preceding this, you have developed the scenario of two clearly identified and separate shooting incidents, and then you go on, in para 330, to state: "The situation does not change, even accepting the hypothesis that the killings are ongoing when Borovcanin passes along the road, no evidence shows that any of Borovcanin's subordinates were inside the warehouse compound at that moment or has been previously discussed in detail -- as has been previously discussed in detail. Borovcanin has no duty, as a superior, to make any inquiries into what was going on in the warehouse unless his men were present there." Now, as I understand it, the situation is that at this time, at least two of the uncontested subordinates of Borovcanin were within -- inside the compound and had been injured or killed, obviously then had been involved in the shootings. Now, if the evidence would be deemed to be that the killings were ongoing when Borovcanin was on the scene, can he then, in a situation like that, walk away without further inquiries into what was going on, not only outside the warehouse, but inside the warehouse? Further, on page 208, you discuss liability under Article 7(1), the commission by omission, or the Blaskic Commission omission liability. And on top of page 215, you first comment on superior responsibility under Article 7(3), and if I understand you well, that is a reference back to the situation we've already mentioned. One exception to this rule, with reference to the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision, one exception is superior responsibility under Article 7(3). That, I understand, is a reference to the other situation. And then you go on to a second exception and with a quote from also the Blaskic Appeal Chamber decision. And then we're into responsibility or possible responsibility under Article 7(1). And you have there, on page 218, in paras 379 and 380, you mention, among other things, the factual basis for this alleged form of responsibility is lacking, and then you go on to say: "The first factual deficiency is that Borovcanin was not necessarily witnessing a crime as he passed by along the road." And then at para 382: "A very real and reasonable possibility exists that the killings had ceased by the time Borovcanin passes the compound." Now, it is possible that here you again premise your discussion on the separate and two clearly-identified separate shootings, but I would also like you, if possible, that you could elaborate what you have said here a little bit more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In respect of the first question, it's important to remember the factual circumstances and the competing factual theories about what happened. Now, it is admitted and conceded that those two individuals were there. But it's also been conceded by the Prosecution, at least, that they were certainly injured and then taken back to the Bratunac Health Clinic. Now, if you accept our sequence of events, and if the first shooting incident was triggered by a break-out attempt, then that means that the first shootings were committed by this prisoner who grabbed the gun, and following that shooting, one of the two MUP soldiers was dead and then the other one was sent back to the clinic. Now, I suggest to you that under those circumstances, you cannot reasonably infer that either of those two individuals committed any crime. And Djukanovic testifies that with the exception of those two specials, he didn't see any other specials inside the warehouse compound. Now, if you accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Gosnell. Perhaps in explaining this, you could also explain one thing. Why would there be those two specials and no one else from the specials?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: A fair question, Your Honour, and a question that we have actually answered in our brief. We do describe that it wasn't unheard of for soldiers to essentially go and wish to speak to prisoners on the basis that they wanted to find out about the fate of relatives, and there was one piece of testimony that said that that's why they went there. Now, I suspect that you're probably skeptical about that explanation, but you also have Djukanovic's direct testimony saying that there weren't any others there. And I suggest that ultimately the burden does fall to the Prosecution to establish that there were other members of the unit there. And when you're considering the evidence about who actually was there, you know that there was a large number of Bratunac Brigade soldiers. So I would simply suggest to you that it's not established beyond a reasonable doubt that anyone more than those two individuals was there. Now, coming back to the question, if you do accept that factual premise as unproven, not our factual premise having been proven, but their factual premise not having been proven that there were others there, and there are no other subordinates in the compound, then that means that there is no 7(3) responsibility at all, and it doesn't matter whether Borovcanin goes back to Bratunac and is told there was a shooting event and other -- and there were non-subordinates participating in that shooting event. He doesn't have a duty, under 7(3). There has to be -- there have to be subordinates to nourish the 7(3) responsibility, and in the absence of that 7(3) foundation, there simply is no obligation, under 7(3), to investigate. So that is -- that is the foundation for our -- for our argument on that issue. Now, as to the second issue, and I believe I have your point, but if I don't, then I hope you'll just interrupt and tell me that I'm wrong and to refocus. The point that I'm trying to make here is that if, in fact, this first shooting incident was a break-out attempt, and we don't know the precise contours of how far it went, in other words, is everybody who -- are all the people who were killed, were they killed lawfully, or did it go a little bit further? Did it go beyond the line of legal suppression of a break-out attempt? I think the point that I'm attempting to make here is that there is a reasonable possibility that all of the killings at that moment that he witnessed were lawful. Or I should again put it more properly: Were not unlawful. Your Honours must make the determination that the Prosecution has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the killings were criminal, and the point that's being made here is that that's not necessarily a safe inference to draw, given what you know about all the facts and the alternative explanation for what might have happened. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I have a question that follows directly upon what the -- the questions posed by Judge Stole. In particular, looking at your brief at page 210, it's paragraph 363 and it's at the very top of the page, and this relates to the Mrksic standard and the Mrksic prerequisites. You make the statement that neither Borovcanin nor any of his men had custody and/or control over all -- I assume you mean over all the 1.000 prisoners held at the Kravica warehouse on the afternoon/evening of the 13th of July, and I'm not clear on this. You've acknowledged it's uncontested that at least two of members of the units under the command of Mr. Borovcanin did have custody of the prisoners not only earlier in the day, but at the Kravica warehouse at one point in time when the shooting incident occurs. I take it you don't dispute that they had custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would dispute that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: You're saying that the two men at the compound, involved in guarding the prisoners who were one injured, one killed, did not have custody of those prisoners at any point in time? I'm not talking about later on. I'm talking at any point in time while they're at the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I would, respectfully, contest that. And the basis for contesting that is twofold. One, mere premise of these two individuals does not mean that they were performing the act of guarding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: They were shot -- one of them was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour, but they -- if you accept the possibility that, essentially, they're off on their own, that these two individuals have gone there to inquire after relatives, and the younger soldier says to the senior one, I want to go there in order to ask these questions. And one of them has a car and drives to that location, of course, they know the location because they were marched from Sandici Meadow to the warehouse. So I suggest that it is a reasonable -- it's a possibility that cannot be excluded as unreasonable that they simply did go there on their own. And I say that not simply in a vacuum of these two gentlemen and suggesting, well, there's evidence in the case that people do this from time to time. I do -- I make that suggestion to you in the broader context of the evidence; namely, that you have two commanders -- at least two people who are commanders of significant-sized units in the Bratunac Brigade, and they're there at the warehouse, and we know that they have at least eight men there at the warehouse. And, further, there's no strong evidence -- there's no reliable evidence at all, virtually no evidence at all, suggesting that the escorting was done by MUP forces. So these are pieces of the puzzle which I respectfully suggest are missing, which might suggest to you that this is not a reliable inference, A, that these two people are there for the purpose of guarding, and, B, that they're part of a larger unit who are present. I think -- so that would be my position on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: All right. Let's presume that there is a conclusion reached that at least two members of Mr. Borovcanin's unit had custody, just for the sake of argument. What is your comment, then, on the Mrksic Appeal Chamber's triggering of a legal duty as a result of that custody, and do you draw any distinction between a commander who may have shared custody of prisoners and then transfers that shared responsibility to another commander, from a commander who has full custody and transfers to another commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that if the -- and of course we're well aware of the facts in Mrksic, and I can -- I know where you're coming from, based upon the facts in Mrksic, but let me just preface my answer to that with this: If the two individuals -- one is dead and one is gone by the time Borovcanin arrives, then I suggest to you -- well, let me back up. The issue of liability for the subordinates is not a matter of omission liability under Mrksic. It is a matter of 7(3) liability. So I would say that when you're arguing in that frame, that's 7(3), and under 7(3), one of them is dead, one of them is gone, I suggest to you that that's the end of the 7(3) responsibility. Now, Mrksic, and I do know the facts of Mrksic, and I understand where you're coming from. First of all, we do have serious legal problems with Mrksic, respectfully submitted. And the second point is that the situation in Mrksic is actually inverted. Remember that in Mrksic, the person who was on trial there and on the basis of those findings, he was the security officer. He had, as I understand it, he had the statutory responsibility which was supposed to be continuous. That was the baseline, that was the default position for custody. So he can't just say, Well, I'm washing my hands of that custody, because it's fixed upon him. And in contrast, and I've quoted from Butler at least five times in our brief, and I apologise if it was repetitive, but that quotation from Butler is so critical to understand what happened here. Borovcanin is not the default position for custody. He is the provisional custodian at the line of combat. That doesn't mean that something couldn't -- that it could have been otherwise. I'm suggesting to you that it's probative of what did happen, especially when you consider that the security organ -- that the chief of the military police and his second in command were all present there, and you have evidence suggesting that Momir Nikolic was actually present at the warehouse at 5.00, not to mention later. So just looking at Mrksic and considering how Mrksic applies to our case, I would suggest that the situation is reversed, and the notion of having to ensure that -- having to ensure that who you're passing prisoners off to is a good custodian, that should be presumed when you're handing off the prisoners to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And I take it -- I understand your response, and I have your point. I take it, though, that there's no suggestion -- by your quote, you're not suggesting that custody necessitates total custody over all of the prisoners, because the way you framed it here, there seem to be some suggestion that it must be over all of the prisoners, and I take it that's not your point. I've understood your point differently. In other words, there can be shared custody between different commanders in different units?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of principle, absolutely, and in fact were concede that in respect of Sandici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have a couple of other points I wanted to raise with you. With respect to the Deserters Unit, which is left at Potocari, I take it, it's not your position, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, that Mr. Borovcanin, in leaving the unit in Potocari, was in any way relieved of his responsibility as a commander of that unit. You don't suggest he was no longer a commander over that unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Not as a formal matter, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Not as a formal matter or a legal matter; he was a commander still of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As long as we understand that term not to imply de facto --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And I'm moving to the next question. It is your position, however, that he no longer had effective command and control, as I read your brief, over that unit. Is it -- is the basis for that -- is it your position that by virtue of leaving the geographic area and leaving his unit in a different geographic area, that that alone results in a loss on the part of the commander of effective command and control of a unit, even for a limited period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's a functional argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps you could just expand a bit on that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's a functional argument, and the claim we make in the brief is that he does not have effective control in respect of the manner in which they are acting and the manner in which they are performing their tasks associated with the evacuation. I think that's an important distinction. Now, I say it's a functional definition, because in militaries -- you've heard many instances during this trial where there's a functional task that a commander is given, and certain units are -- or people, resources, are provided to that person to perform that task. And I suggest to you that when that suggestion arises, whoever has the actual capacity to issue orders in relation of that function, that's the person who has effective control. There is a principle of unity of command, and I suggest that when you have that functional designation which comes from Mladic, it comes from Jankovic, it flows to Momir Nikolic, and then you have all kinds of evidence of him, on the ground, issuing orders, then that is a functionally-defined assumption of command and control over those individuals. So I wouldn't say it was a geographical issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And you're not suggesting he, at any point in time, had relinquished his command responsibility, distinct from control?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As a formal matter, he did remain the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Throughout?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, throughout that day. I do believe at some point I would say that it ceases, but that's outside of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one final point on the issue that you raised regarding my questions yesterday to Mr. Bourgon on the question of the detention of the population, and I've read your brief on the point. I am fairly certain I know your answer to this question, but the additional element in the question yesterday is movement of those individuals who are detained, and I take it from your comments that you would say detention, including movement, is permissible; what's significant is the period of time. Is that your position? So that it is lawful to both detain and move the individuals?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't wish to take a position on the movement between Bratunac and Zvornik. That issue -- I'm only making -- because the movement that occurred on the 12th and 13th was between Potocari and Bratunac, and I would suggest that there's absolutely nothing [Realtime transcript read in error "absolutely improper"] improper in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay. So confining it to that particular movement, you'd say that that is part of the detention that is perfectly lawful?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would say so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I haven't really heard you give a clear explanation or response to the comment or remark made by Mr. McCloskey; namely, that had the alleged attempted escape really occurred, then that would have been one of the first things that your client would have mentioned when he was interviewed by the Prosecution, but he never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, two points on this. I would actually refer you back to the interview, itself, and see how my client responds, and see the skepticism that you see in response from the questioner, see whether there were any additional questions, whether there was any opening for him to give an answer about that particular potential scenario. You'll see that there's very little -- he has very little opening to discuss that, given the nature of the interview, given the nature of the questions, given the presumptions of the interviewer that were being telegraphed very strongly during the interview. And there's absolutely nothing wrong with that, Your Honour, but that was the atmosphere of the interview. And the second point is it presumes that my client, in 2002, had full knowledge of exactly what happened, and I suggest to you that that's simply not a safe assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That concludes the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just say -- I didn't say this at the end of my closing remarks, but I wish to tell you that it has been a privilege to appear before you and among such distinguished and excellent colleagues, and the professionalism also around the courtroom of everybody who is involved in the process has been tremendous, and including stenographers, interpreters, legal officers, Registry. It has been a pleasure. And I wish to adjust one note on behalf of my client, who particularly wishes to thank the courtesy and professionalism of the security staff who have been accompanying him for the duration of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure these words are appreciated. Ms. Fauveau, I suppose you start after the break. We'll have the break straight now, so it's 25 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry to detain you with this, Mr. President, but three transcript corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yesterday, 34570, line 8, it should read "from page 34325." Today, page 7, line 3, the footnote referred to is "4408." At page 28 of today's transcript, line 20, the phrase should be "absolutely nothing improper." Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. One moment, Ms. Fauveau. Okay. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, at the close of this trial the Prosecution's final brief and their oral arguments are the best evidence of the Prosecution's inability to establish the responsibility of General Miletic. Both their final brief and the oral arguments are based on mis-characterisation and an artificial interpretation of evidence, as well as on blatantly incorrect solutions. To start with, let me say a few words about the plan that was allegedly envisaged by the military and political Serb leadership in 1992, and that allegedly was applied throughout the war. I do not intend to dwell on this period, which is outside the indictment, but the Prosecution's conclusions referring thereto, which somehow incriminate the entire VRS and even the entire Serb people, cannot be left unanswered. At paragraph 68 of their closing brief, the Prosecution quotes Colonel Lasic as saying that the main objective of the VRS was to defend the Serb population, and if there was no other solution available, then to separate peoples on ethnic principles. The conclusion drawn by the Prosecution is that the objective of the VRS was the forcible transfer of Muslims or ethnic cleansing. This is a misstatement. This conclusion is incorrect because Colonel Lasic was not speaking about forcibly transferring Muslims. The allegation that the very objective of the VRS was to transfer population or ethnically cleanse the population would mean that the VRS was, in and of itself, a criminal organisation and that, therefore, each and every VRS member, by the mere fact that they belonged to the VRS, was a member of a criminal enterprise. This is obviously not the case. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was ethnic by nature, which has been acknowledged by the Prosecutor, himself, in paragraph 165 of their final brief. Those who were unlucky enough to experience a war know that contrary to what General Smith would like us to believe, war is nothing but immense suffering. What brings nothing but fear, pain, and tragedy. It is common knowledge that forcible transfer is banned in law, but Colonel Lasic was not speaking about forcible transfer. He was speaking about separating peoples at war, a separation which should have limited suffering when there was no other alternative possible any longer. I would like to recall that in an advisory opinion, the permanent Court of International Justice wrote in 1930, in the case of the Greco-Bulgarian Communities that, I quote: "The general purpose of this instrument is thus: By as wide a measure of reciprocal emigration as possible, to eliminate or reduce in the Balkans the centres of irredentist agitation, which was shown by the history of the preceding periods to have been so often the cause of lamentable incidents or serious conflicts, and to render more effective than in the past the process of pacification in the countries of Eastern Europe." This opinion was about the Balkans and the tragic events experienced by the peoples in the Balkans throughout the 20th century, and in the war that broke out in 1990 in the former Yugoslavia shows, even 80 years later, how wise the opinion was. The policy of a people and of its army cannot be assessed broadly, generally, in a vacuum. It must be placed in its own historical and social context. In this context, the separation Colonel Lasic was speaking about did not mean moving population. It meant the creation of distinct entities, the Serb entity and the Muslim entity, which was eventually achieved with the signing of the Dayton Accords. At the end of the 20th century, Yugoslavia broke up into several states. The foundation of this break-up was ethnicity. The Soviet Union broke up on the same ethnic lines, and so was the case with Czechoslovakia. Like anywhere else, the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina no longer wanted to live in one-and-the-same state. The war did not break out because the Serbs and the Muslims did not want to live in a common state, but because they were not able to reach an agreement and to part in peace. Forcible transfer is a crime. Separating peoples is a way of avoiding war, suffering, and tragedy. Colonel Lasic had this type of separation in mind when he spoke. War cannot be and is not an excuse for crimes, and those who commit crimes have to answer for them. However, the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, was not a criminal organisation. It was an army of the Serbian people in Bosnia. The fact that General Miletic was part of the VRS is, in itself, of no importance, of no significance. General Miletic, just as many members of the VRS, had no criminal intent. He did not intend to forcibly transfer the Muslim population, and he did not at all want to take part in any such enterprise. Let me now address some of the Prosecutor's allegations that not only fail to be supported by any evidence whatsoever, but also squarely fall outside the scope of the indictment with regard to General Miletic, and this calls for a few preliminary remarks. When the Prosecutor sought to join cases, the Miletic Defence opposed the motion, as it found the indictment, if it were to be joined, was confused and, as such, was prejudicial to the accused, because faced with a confused indictment, an accused is not in a position to understand the nature and the cause of the charges against him. The Miletic Defence also filed a preliminary motion in which it underscored that the indictment was not clear enough as to whether General Miletic was charged with taking part in a single criminal enterprise or in the two criminal enterprises alleged in the indictment. After the Miletic Defence filed their motion, the Trial Chamber issued a decision on the 31st of May, 2006, in which it held that paragraph 47 -- at paragraph 47 that General Miletic was accused as a member of the JCE aiming at the forcible transfer of the Muslim population, and that he was accused solely as a member of that criminal enterprise. The Prosecutor did not appeal the decision. Paragraph 97 of the indictment was mentioned by the Prosecutor in support of their case that General Miletic was allegedly a member of the JCE aiming at committing murders, and that it was identical to Annex A in the indictment. That was the object of our preliminary motion and of your decision of 31st of May, 2006. An accused is not a member of a JCE because it is so alleged in an indictment. It must be proven that an accused was a member of a joint criminal enterprise. The presumption of innocence is the very foundation of any criminal proceeding. It is enshrined in Article 21.3 of the Statute of our Tribunal. The Prosecution case that General Miletic was allegedly a member of a criminal -- a joint criminal enterprise that aimed at committing murders, although he was not charged with participating in such a criminal enterprise, disregards every single principle of criminal law, flies in the face of any legal reasoning, and is not permissible. The established case law requires that an indictment contain specific charges, and taking into account the 31st of May, 2006 decision, the paragraphs of the Prosecution's final brief referring to the alleged participation of General Miletic in the JCE aiming at murders must squarely be disregarded. Neither the murders in Nezuk, neither the murders of Muslims taken to the Milici hospital, or the transfer of bodies to secondary graves are part of the charges against General Miletic. The allegations regarding the above acts may not be taken into account to establish the criminal intent of General Miletic, because as was held by the Trial Chamber in the Djordjevic case, intent can be inferred only from facts that are clearly alleged in the indictment. Equally, the Prosecutor may not now infer General Miletic intent from the knowledge he allegedly had of acts and conducts prior to March 1995. If the Prosecutor sought to prove his intention through events that were prior to the 8th of March, 1995, the Prosecutor had to say so in the indictment, which he did not do. It was not done either in the pre-trial brief or in the opening statement. Further to the Appeals Chamber established case law, the Prosecutor is not allowed to change his case without formally seeking leave to amend the indictment if the trial proceedings, as they progress, do not confirm the Prosecution's initial case. Equally, the Trial Chamber is not allowed to base its findings on facts that have not been properly alleged in the indictment. Let me say a few words about the section of the Prosecution's final brief about the Muslim column that left Srebrenica. At paragraph 1700, the Prosecutor makes allegations on the part played by General Miletic in the follow-up of the Muslim column. At the hearing of the 3rd of September, 2009, the Prosecutor expressed their novel, previously unheard of position that the column and the people in the column were part of a forcible transfer. I shall not repeat the arguments showing that this column was a legitimate military target, which was confirmed, by the way, even by the Prosecutor's military expert, Richard Butler, on the 23rd of January, 2008; transcript pages 20244 and 20245. I wish to underscore the Prosecutor's statements, who said, on two occasions, in no uncertain terms, that this column was, indeed, a military column, that it attacked Serbian positions, and especially that it was not part of the indictment. This was said on the 1st of November, 2006, page 3382, and on the 7th of February, 2007, transcript page 7041. The Prosecutor's interpretation of the facts at the hearing of the 3rd of September, 2009, runs contrary to the testimony of Richard Butler, who testified that in spite of the presence of civilians in the column, the column was a legitimate military target. But even more serious than that, this new interpretation by the Prosecutor stands in contradiction to the Prosecutor's very statement regarding the column. The Prosecution cannot change tacks as it suits them. If the acts aimed at neutralising militarily the column are to be interpreted as a contribution to JCE, the Prosecutor should not have said that the column was not part of the indictment. The entire -- the accused is entitled to know the charges against him, and when the Prosecutor said, on the record, that the column was not part of the indictment, how could the accused surmise that the Prosecutor would change their case in their closing arguments? But that's not all. The Prosecutor, lacking any evidence against General Miletic, is now trying to incriminate him for other facts that have never been alleged. The Prosecutor never alleged that General Miletic played any part in requisitioning the buses that were to transport the population. However, in their closing brief, the Prosecution is seeking to accuse General Miletic of mobilising, of requisitioning. Of course, there is no evidence to show any link between General Miletic and the requisitioning operation. But if the allegation was part of the alleged contribution of General Miletic to the JCE, it should have been stated expressly in the indictment. The same applies to the arms supplied to Drina Corps units during the Krivaja operation. There is no evidence to support the Prosecution's case. But further than that, the Prosecutor never alleged that General Miletic was in any way involved in supplying weapons. Also, the Prosecutor never alleged that General Miletic or the officers of the operations organ were in any way involved in drafting the orders of the 10th and the 13th of July, 1995. These are Exhibits P181 and P45. Drafting orders is no evidence; it is a material fact, just as requisitioning is, just as supplying arms is. A possible participation by General Miletic in these acts could be found as the accused's contribution to JCE. However, if such acts are to represent General Miletic's alleged contribution to the JCE, they should have been set out expressly in the indictment, and they were not. Neither were they in the pre-trial brief or the opening statements. Even during Rule 98 bis arguments at the end of the Prosecution case, the Prosecutor never alleged that General Miletic did in any way take part in drafting the orders, in requisitioning buses, and in supplying the Drina Corps units with weapons. Furthermore, on several occasions in their final brief, the Prosecution alleged that the officers of operations -- for operations subordinated to General Miletic committed certain acts. With regard to General Miletic's responsibility, his alleged participation in JCE, the Prosecutor must prove that he had a personal contribution to it through his personal and individual acts. What other officers may have done, even if they were General Miletic's subordinates, may not be held against him for the sake of his participation to the joint criminal enterprise. Lastly, allow me a few remarks on paragraph 75(B) and (C) of the indictment. These paragraphs contain the English word "monitor." This word has always been translated into B/C/S -- into the B/C/S version of the indictment with the word "supervise." At the hearing of the 26th of November, 2008, the Prosecutor explained that this was not about supervision, but about follow-up. However, the Prosecutor never sought to correct the B/C/S version of the indictment. He just said that B/C/S is not an official language of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. For the record, I think, because it will be better, what's the word in B/C/S that is used in the B/C/S version of the indictment, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "Nadzirati," n-a-d-z-i-r-a-t-i. The rules governing official languages do not apply here. What applies is Article 21.4.A of the Statute that guarantees that the accused is entitled to know the nature and the cause of the charges in a language that he understands. To the extent that General Miletic could understand the indictment, he was charged with supervising specific activities. A new term was used in November 2008, over two years after the commencement of the trial, and this is obviously prejudicial to the accused. Furthermore, this change was made after the testimony of two Defence witnesses, who confirmed that General Miletic was not in charge of supervising the activities of VRS units or of supervising the activities of enemy units. These were Ljubomir Obradovic, 17th of November, 2008, transcript pages 28288 and 28295; and Novica Simic, 19th of November, 2008, transcript pages 28511. The indictment is a Prosecution instrument. The Prosecutor should have made sure that the B/C/S translation met their intentions. The word "monitor" can be translated in two ways into B/C/S, by the word "supervising" or the word "follow-up." So this is not a translation error. This is about an ambiguous term used by the Prosecutor that cannot be held or interpreted to the detriment of the accused. Before analysing the case against General Miletic, I'd like to say a few words about the evidence. First of all, I'd like to speak about the testimony of General Milovanovic. Basically, the entire Prosecution case against General Miletic, and especially the section regarding the post and position of General Miletic, as well as his role in drafting Directive number 7, rely on the testimony of General Milovanovic. General Milovanovic is a Prosecution witness. However, even the Prosecutor challenged his credibility when it came to Directive number 4, in their brief, and Directive number 7 at the hearing of 2nd of September, 2009. We agree with the Prosecutor here, when he says that the testimony of General Milovanovic lacks credibility with regard to the directives, but we also believe that General Milovanovic is not credible when he speaks about the duties and the position of General Miletic. The reason why he testified is simply that he was seeking to elude or at least minimise his own potential responsibility. Unfortunately, when General Milovanovic testified, the Defence did not have in their possession documents showing that he was present, he being General Milovanovic, he was present at the Main Staff headquarters in the spring of 1995. The Defence did not have documents showing that he was fully cognizance of Directive number 7 and showing acts that he undertook in the Drina Corps area of responsibility and until the 1st of June, 1995. All these documents were obtained much later. The key document, which is the diary of President Karadzic's secretary, was obtained only in September 2008. Indeed, a large amount of documents, most of which were favourable to the Defence, were obtained in this trial at a very late stage of the proceedings. We do regret the situation, but I'd like to underline that we do not mean to say that the Prosecutor behaved improperly. With regard to the other evidence, I'd like to dwell for a moment on intercepts that are a considerable part of the case file. They must be assessed with the utmost care, especially when the intercepts contain remarks showing that there are disruptions or changes in voices. We also must pay particular care to dates, names of participants, and the names of people being mentioned. Errors cannot be ruled out. The remarks on disruptions and changes in voices show that audibility and, therefore, understanding conversations was a difficult task, therefore, the margin or likelihood of errors in these conversations is higher. The content of an intercept that was not corroborated by other evidence should be disregarded. Let me remind you the testimony of PW-147, an operator who admitted that in specific situations the events that actually took place were the opposite of what had been noted in the conversation. This was said on the 24th of January, 2007, transcript pages 6329/6330. Even though the case law does not require testimony to be corroborated, this is necessary for testimony under 92 bis when the author of the statement is not called to testify and when the witness could not be cross-examined. Elements of such a statement cannot lead to a finding of guilt if they are not corroborated. I would like to deal with a point of law that we raised in paragraph 610 and 611, which has to do with the -- with deporting the Muslim men from Zepa. These arguments have been set out regarding Zepa. They apply as well to the column that left from Srebrenica and to forcible transfer that would - according to the new positions taken by the Prosecutor - that would apply to the column. As said in our brief, we took note of the case law for victims of crimes against humanity, but I hail from civil law and I find it somewhat difficult to accept this position. Criminal law calls for a restrictive and strict interpretation. The Statute of this Tribunal has the force of law. Article 5 of the Statute imposes general conditions that have to be met for any crime against humanity. The Article provides that the International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons held responsible for the following crimes, when committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal in character, and directed against any civilian population. Article 5 is different from the provisions that can be found in other international texts regarding crimes against humanity, including in the Statute for the ICTR and the Statute of the ICC, which require that crimes must be committed as part of a general, wide-scale, and systematic attack, that's for the ICTR, and large-scale and systematic for the ICC. In this Tribunal, the requirement of a systematic or wide-scale attack was added by jurisprudence as a necessary requirement for the crime to be a crime against humanity. This is understandable, but this does not prejudice the accused, and this is not outside a restrictive interpretation of the law. However, this generalised or systematic attack is a requirement established by case law. It is not a statutory requirement. Article 5 of the Statute makes no mention of a generalised or systematic attack. The only mention is a mention of an armed conflict. Since there is no mention of attack in the wording, the civilian population mentioned in Article 5 cannot be the target of the attack, but only of crimes that are mentioned in the wording. This Article, at least in its French version, requires that crimes be directed against a civilian population. This being said, let me specify that we are of the view that the presence of a few military inside a civilian population is not going to change anything to the civilian character of the population, but also that a military unit or a group of combatants able to fight that would be totally separated from the civilian population cannot be held as victims of a crime against humanity, as set out in the ICTY Statute. With regard to the column that left from Srebrenica, those who joined the column did so in order to contribute to the military actions, which was the break-out of the 28th Division from Srebrenica towards Central Bosnia. As they had joined a military formation, they became combatants. This applies to the members of the 285 Brigade of Zepa and those who joined them. Both the 28th Division and the 285th Brigade left Srebrenica and Zepa with the intent of joining or going to Muslim-held territory and, if need be, to fight the Serb forces. Activities by Serb forces directed against such groups were purely military activities. Before I move to analyse the alleged participation of General Miletic in the JCE, I want to stress that there is no evidence showing that General Miletic ordered or planned the alleged crimes, which has been alleged by the Prosecution in their brief. Although the Prosecutor hinted that a host of documents transmitted by General Miletic incurred his responsibility for ordering criminal acts, the Prosecution failed to specify a single order or a crime that would have resulted from carrying out such an order. If, further to the Tribunal's case law, a person can be held responsible for ordering, even if that said person did nothing but transmit the order, and if the order was not issued in a particular form, the Prosecutor has to specify the particular order giving rise to the accused's responsibility for ordering a criminal offence that would constitute a crime under the Tribunal's Statute. The Prosecution must also prove that the order was unlawful and had been transmitted in the knowledge that a crime could have been committed in carrying out the said order. Finally, the Prosecutor must prove that the ordered crime was, indeed, committed. In the present case, the Prosecutor has failed to adduce any evidence that General Miletic ever ordered a crime. At paragraphs 1741 and 1743 of their brief, the Prosecution alleged that General Miletic planned the crimes. Paragraph 1743 is, in and of itself, contradictory because the Prosecutor first alleged that General Miletic assisted in planning the crimes, only to say later that he had a central role in planning the strategy that was later implemented by the RS and VRS leadership which eventually led to the enclaves being taken and the population -- the Muslim population being moved. First of all, planning a crime and planning a strategy that may have led to a crime being committed are two very different things. The first implies the direct planning of a criminal act; for instance, moving the population. The second, in terms of planning an act that is perfectly lawful, but then later led to a crime being committed, planning a strategy that led to the commission of a crime is not planning as understood in Article 7(1) of the Statute, but it can be tantamount to contributing to a joint criminal enterprise. There is no evidence in the case file to support the case that General Miletic planned criminal acts. Later on, I shall return to the role General Miletic played in drafting Directive number 7, but for the time being let me just say that the case that General Miletic planned the strategy that was later implemented by the RS leadership is totally illogical. It is obvious that the strategy applied by the political and military leaders could only be planned by the latter, and certainly not by an officer who was not among the leaders. The Prosecutor tells you that he does not seek the conviction of General Miletic because he was the chief of the Administration for Operational Affairs and Training in the VRS, but that's precisely what the Prosecutor does. He accused precisely General Miletic and solely because of the position he held. Look at the entire case against General Miletic. The Prosecutor's brief, their closing arguments, everything relies on the phrase that "he should have known." Only last Friday, page 34279, the Prosecutor said the following sentence: "It is inconceivable for the chiefs of operation not to know." But that's not the question at issue, and it should not be the question at issue for a criminal trial. But let's start with the beginning, and it must be said that the Prosecutor mis-characterised the position held by General Miletic throughout the war. For instance, it emerges from paragraph 69 of the Prosecutor's brief that Colonel Lasic was subordinate to General Miletic. The Prosecutor refers to not a single shred of evidence confirming this, and he could not have, because Colonel Lasic left the Department for Operations of the Main Staff on the 21st of May, 1993, was never subordinated to General Miletic. This is confirmed by Exhibit P3178. Also, the Prosecutor claims at paragraph 1662 of their brief that General Miletic was the assistant chief for operations before he became the chief of operations in June 1993. First of all, the position of chief of operations is not known within the VRS, and it is impossible to understand whether the Prosecutor had in mind the chief of Administration for Operations and Training or the chief of the Department for Operations. It must be said, for the Prosecutor, that General Milovanovic, whose testimony was mentioned by the Prosecutor, was very vague on this point. However, concrete evidence of the position held by General Miletic is given by Exhibit P3178. It shows clearly that General Miletic was never the assistant chief for the Administration of Operations and Training and that he never held any position or duties in the Department for Operations. Exhibit P3178 is credible evidence that was, by the way, referred to on many occasions by the Prosecutor. At paragraph 1662, the Prosecutor alleged that General Miletic was in the organs for operations at the time Directive 4 was drafted and also at the time when there were military activities in Cerska, end of 1992, beginning of 1993, but such allegations are not supported by any evidence and run contrary to this exhibit I have already mentioned, P3178. The Prosecutor also claims that General Miletic was involved in drafting the analysis on combat readiness for the year 1992 and that he had to help his superior, Dragutin Ilic, draft the analysis. The Prosecutor refers to Richard Butler, who testified that General Miletic was subordinated to Dragutin Ilic, but who never said that he was involved in drafting the analysis. Furthermore, what General Miletic had to do was of no significance. The Prosecutor should have proven what General Miletic actually did, but the Prosecutor failed to prove any involvement of General Miletic in drafting the analysis on combat readiness for the year 1992. The Prosecutor alleged -- made allegations about the duration of General Miletic's participation in Operation Spring. It was wrong. Dragisa Masal said that the operation lasted, at most, one week to ten days. He said so on the 2nd of December, 2008, transcript pages 29143. Indeed, the Operation Spring lasted exactly five days, from the 3rd to the 8th of May, 1993. The 1st of May, 1993 order, Exhibit P2742, mentioned by the Prosecutor shows that the operation started on the 3rd of May, and the operation did, indeed, end with the creation of the safe area in Zepa on the 8th of May, 1993, which has been acknowledged by the Prosecutor. Let us look at the meaning of this 1st of May order and what General Miletic may have understood of it. In paragraph 16 -- the Prosecutor reaches a conclusion that is obviously wrong when he says that the order given by General Miletic on the 1st of May, 1993, is an attempt to reach the third strategic objective, which is to move Muslims out of the Drina Valley. The 1st of May, 1993 order is not an order given by the man who was then Colonel Miletic; it is an order by General Milovanovic. Furthermore, the Prosecutor concluded that this operation aimed at deporting or transferring Muslims, and this is not a reasonable conclusion; quite the contrary. The sole objective of this order is clearly spelled out in the points -- items 4 and 5. It was exclusively to attack the Muslim forces. The order provided for the possibility for the Muslim population to stay or to leave for Central Bosnia. This possibility did not mean that the population would be forcibly transferred. Movement of population was not necessarily the objective of the attack. It was often the consequence of military activities and of the change of rule. In the 1st of May, 1993 order, this possibility was foreseen, but it was not envisaged with the aim of forcing the population to leave, but in order to make sure that it would be safe if it decided to leave. The Prosecutor acknowledges that the attack in Zepa in May 1993 ended with the creation of the safe area. Together with the safe area being created, Zepa should have been demilitarised. It is obvious that the VRS thought that the objectives of the Spring operation had been achieved with the zone being demilitarised, which is something the VRS Main Staff believed in at the time. The end of military activity, when the zone was demilitarised, shows that the purpose of the operation was not to transfer population; that it was, indeed, to neutralise Muslim forces, which is a natural and legitimate objective in any armed conflict. Directive number 6, Exhibit P3919, also shows that transfer of the Muslim population was not an objective of the VRS. This directive was issued in 1993, after the demilitarised zones were created, and it did not mention the Drina Valley among the objectives of the VRS. Demilitarisation of the zones under Muslim rule in the Drina Valley was the purpose of all the VRS activities in the zone. The documents of the VRS cannot be interpreted in a vacuum or in the light of events that occurred two years later. Any document must be assessed in the context in which it was written. The possibility was given to civilian population to go in the order of the 1st of May, but it was not expressing an intention to transfer the Muslim population; it only expressed the fact that a population often follows their army. So contrary to the Prosecutor's allegation, the sentence shows that when the order was drafted, all the steps were taken to ensure the safety of the civilian population.
