The way the Prosecutor interpreted this order shows that the Prosecutor totally disregards the armed conflict, the objective of which was to defeat the enemy forces. Contrary to the Prosecutor's conclusion, there can be no unlawful meaning to be attributed to VRS documents when there is a reasonable military explanation. The 1st of May, 1993 order is a military document that is perfectly regular and lawful that allows for no other interpretation. The participation of General Miletic in the Spring operation was militarily justified, was perfectly lawful. No criminal intent can be inferred therefrom. The way the Prosecutor interpreted the 1st of May, 1993 order is very relevant, and, indeed, the Prosecutor endeavours to assign to all VRS documents, regardless of their actual contents and objectives, an unlawful purpose because it -- the Prosecutor interprets them ex post de facto, seeking in them a harbinger of tragic events that took place in July 1995. Such an approach is not helpful for the Trial Chamber because the Trial Chamber cannot infer criminal intent from an act if there is another reasonable conclusion. The Prosecution identifies General Miletic with Main Staff and attributes all Main Staff actions to General Miletic. Throughout the trial, the Prosecutor sought to position General Miletic at a post or a position that was not his and to ascribe to him knowledge regarding the situation on the front, insubordinate units in the sector of intelligence, logistics, mobilisation, and in any other facet of the work done by the VRS, knowledge that went way beyond the commander's actual knowledge. Obviously, this case cannot be supported and is not supported by any single evidence, and it is totally wrong. General Miletic is not the Main Staff. His possible contribution to the alleged JCE can only be assessed on the basis of his own conduct. The acts by the Main Staff cannot be ascribed to General Miletic unless they are acts in which his participation has been established. General Miletic was not the commander of the Main Staff. He was not supposed to know everything that may have happened at the level of the Main Staff. He cannot be held responsible for each and every action by the Main Staff. Whatever the position and the duties held by General Miletic, the function, the position, in and of itself, cannot be the evidence of his alleged membership in the JCE, nor of his alleged contribution to it. The Prosecutor spent a large part of this trial and of his final brief to the general's duties in order to conceal the paucity of evidence they had to prove his alleged criminal responsibility. I am not going to address the arguments we have in our final brief as to his duties. They show clearly that General Miletic never had the authority and the powers of the chief of staff and that never he was the main advisor to General Mladic. I shall just underline some of the Prosecutor's conclusions that are totally unfounded. When he tried to explain what General Miletic's duty was, the Prosecutor referred mainly to General Milovanovic's testimony. In paragraph 635 to 653, the Prosecutor mentioned General Milovanovic 25 times. But the Prosecutor says so, himself; he said that General Milovanovic was not a credible witness. And when the Prosecutor does not refer to General Milovanovic, he quotes the regulation, 7DP410, applicable to corps -- army corps, whereas corps are units with a structure, organisation, and operation that are very different from those of the Main Staff. So this evidence is just as inclusive as General Milovanovic's testimony when it comes to General Miletic's responsibility. This evidence fails to reflect the true duties of General Miletic, do not allow to infer what he really did. This evidence says nothing as to his tasks at the time of the activities around Srebrenica and Zepa. When the commander, the chief of staff, and many assistant commanders were absent from the Main Staff, and when the situation was very remote from the regular situation described by General Milovanovic, and was very different from the situation set out in the above-mentioned regulations, let it be noted that the regulation applied to corps units and also that they were to be applied in peacetime. You will find an illustration of the utter uselessness of this evidence in the Prosecutor's allegation that General Miletic should have made suggestions to General Mladic as to the way to engage the units. Not surprisingly, the evidence quoted by the Prosecutor is General Milovanovic's testimony. However, what matters in this trial is not whether General Miletic could or should have suggested the way to engage units, but whether he did so for the Drina Corps units for the period from March to August 1995. There is no single piece of evidence to confirm that General Miletic would have done so. There is, indeed, no evidence that General Miletic made any suggestion at all to General Mladic or that General Mladic ever consulted him. General Milovanovic was General Mladic's confidant throughout the war. He said so himself. General Mladic, himself, acknowledged at the end of the war that General Milovanovic held a privileged position. He made a speech at the beginning of 1996 in which General Mladic expressed his gratitude and his thankfulness to General Milovanovic in the following terms: "Once again, a special thank you to you, General Milovanovic, in particular, my right hand, who very successfully stood in for me at all difficult moments and helped me enormously." At the hearing of 7 of September, the Prosecutor stated that the presence of General Milovanovic at the Main Staff headquarters did not change much as to the position held by General Miletic. However, in paragraph 11 of the indictment, the Prosecutor described General Miletic as the main advisor to General Mladic precisely because he represented General Milovanovic. But if General Milovanovic was present at the Main Staff headquarters, nobody could have represented him. The Defence contends that General Miletic was never General Mladic's main advisor, whether Milovanovic was present or not. However, the statement by the Prosecutor that the return of General Milovanovic changed nothing to the situation for General Miletic is, in the ambit of the Prosecutor's case against General Miletic, devoid of any logic. Furthermore, the Prosecutor uses different methods to assess the role of General Miletic and the role played by General Milovanovic. If the Prosecutor is to be believed, the mere fact that General Milovanovic left the Main Staff headquarters would exonerate him of any responsibility, although he was sent on the ground precisely to assess the situation and precisely in order to gather information that he would take to General Mladic. On the other hand, it is said that General Miletic, even when he's on leave in Belgrade, could have sought to be informed as to the situation. This is absurd, especially so if you factor in that General Milovanovic was, without the shadow of a doubt and throughout the war, the main associate -- the closest associate, the most appreciated associate of General Mladic. It is not disputed that General Miletic worked with Milovanovic. He was subordinated to General Milovanovic. But this is of no assistance to the Prosecutor, because General Milovanovic, under the indictment, is not a member of the joint criminal enterprise. General Miletic never found himself in the position of General Milovanovic. Therefore, it is certain that General Mladic did not inform him of any planned or decided military action.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: (redacted). The Prosecutor fully disregards differences in activities that happened at various levels, at strategic, operational, and tactical levels, and contrary to all evidence, assigns the same role to General Miletic, whatever the action may have been. General Miletic did not belong to the inner circle of the Main Staff. He was not part of the decision-making process. General Mladic did not mention him as one of his close associates in the speech he made at the end of the war. This is Exhibit 5D1441. The Prosecutor remained silent regarding General Mladic's speech, although the speech is crucial evidence when it comes to assessing the parts played by General Miletic. General Mladic was speaking in front of his associates, in front of officers who knew what roles the members of the Main Staff played, and in front of people in front of which he had no reason not to mention his close associates. General Miletic was present when General Mladic made the speech, and if he had been one of his close associates, it is sure that General Mladic would not have forgotten to mention him. Since General Miletic was not among the inner circles of General Mladic's closest team workers, team members, it is hard to imagine that he may have been in the unique position of advising General Mladic. Indeed, for General Miletic to be in the position of providing advice to General Mladic, it would have been necessary for Mladic to give him the opportunity to do so, therefore, to ask him for advice. The Prosecutor failed to provide any evidence that General Mladic ever addressed or turned to General Miletic for advice or that General Miletic ever provided such advice. The only such piece of evidence is document 5D1016, a 1994 document. However, in this document General Miletic did nothing but pass on to General Mladic a proposal made by the Drina Corps commander. Furthermore, this document shows that General Mladic did not accept the proposal made by the Drina Corps commander and that he had a different opinion than General Miletic or, rather, that General Miletic did not agree with General Mladic's decision. At paragraph 1650, the Prosecutor alleges that the influence of General Miletic in the Main Staff increased and that his proposals were complied with, were accepted. All this is not supported by evidence. General Miletic was the only general in the Main Staff who was not mentioned expressly in General Mladic's speech at the end of the war. Furthermore, the conversation between General Mladic and General Tolimir on the 24th of July, 1995 - this is Exhibit P1327 - is a good indicator of the degree to which General Mladic would respect and accept proposals made by General Miletic. In this conversation, General Mladic did not even take into account the opinion expressed by General Miletic, and he ordered precisely the opposite to General Tolimir. Equally, the Prosecutor has no evidence to substantiate his allegations that General Miletic had an essential role in each of the decisions taken to further the objective of the alleged JCE and that General Miletic's decisions were crucial in the efforts undertaken to defeat, militarily, the Muslim forces and to transfer the Muslim population out of Srebrenica and Zepa. The Prosecutor fails to refer to any decision by General Miletic. He can't do so because there is no such thing as a decision issued by General Miletic. At paragraph 131 of their brief, the Prosecution quoted General Nicolai, who testified that the answers -- useful answers to the VRS Main Staff could be obtained only from generals because generals were probably the only one authorised to make any decisions. General Miletic was a colonel until the end of June 1995. Therefore, if General Nicolai is to be believed, and supposedly the Prosecutor believed him because he quoted him, General Miletic, at least until the end of June 1995, at least until the end of June 1995, could not have played any essential role in the decision-making process. General Mladic was the commander of the VRS and is certainly better placed than General Nicolai to say who, within the Main Staff, took part in the decision-making process. That's precisely what he did. In this speech that I've mentioned several times, General Mladic listed the officers who took part in taking decisions. In doing so, he made no mention of General Miletic. Let me now address the issue of humanitarian aid before I tackle the issue of the directive, because I think there is no link between the two. First of all, there is no evidence of a specific policy by the VRS regarding the supply of humanitarian aid to the Eastern Bosnian enclaves. With regard to humanitarian aid, the Defence found themselves in a quandary because, as was stated in our brief, and as you've noted yourselves, certain important facts that were unfavorable to the Defence were taken judicial notice of, and the position for the Defence was even more difficult because documents regarding humanitarian aid are held by organisations that are in no obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal. We are all aware of the position adopted by international humanitarian organisations when it comes to producing their documents, and there's no need to dwell on the issue. However, although the Defence had the burden of adducing evidence to refute facts and judicial notice, the Prosecutor had the burden of proof beyond any reasonable doubt, yet the evidence adduced at trial cast a serious doubt on the Prosecution's allegation. The evidence adduced at trial no longer allowed the finding that in early 1995 there were less and less humanitarian convoys that reached Srebrenica. It is no longer possible to find that the Bosnian Serbs deliberately tried to impede access to enclaves and that blocking humanitarian convoys was part of a plan. You have a chart on page 21 of Exhibit P4145. It proves beyond all reasonable doubt that humanitarian aid was supplied to the Eastern Bosnian enclaves, including Srebrenica and Zepa, on a regular basis until June 1995. There was no reduction that would have resulted from the Directive number 7 being issued. This exhibit, P4145, is undoubtedly the best evidence with regard to the humanitarian aid supplied to the enclaves. This exhibit proves that the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves were better supplied than the other enclaves in Bosnia, that the aid supplied in March, April, and May 1995 actually increased compared to February 1995, and that, at any rate, in 1995, until June 1995, it was supplied much more regularly than it was in 1994. Exhibit P4145 is a document that comes from the organisation that is best positioned to know the situation, in terms of humanitarian aid, and the volumes of humanitarian aid provided. It would not make sense to disregard this exhibit for the sake of testimony that, in the light of this exhibit, appeared to be totally wrong. I can only regret that this international organisation did not wish to let the Defence access their archives. The requests made to the Serbian authorities and the answers could not be accessed, either. These are documents that could have demonstrated with even more cogency that there was no plan to restrict humanitarian aid. This testimony referred to by the Prosecutor in support of their case is evidence that in the absence of further evidence, led this Tribunal to determine in previous cases that humanitarian aid had been deliberately restricted as of the beginning of 1995. I'm speaking of the testimony of DutchBat members, of Johannes [as interpreted] Rutten, for instance, who can only remember a single UNHCR convoy in 1995, whilst Exhibit P4145 shows us that 11 convoys reached the enclave. Witness Rutten does not remember a single UNHCR convoy in April, whilst there were 10 that brought larger quantities of humanitarian aid than the 11 convoys in March. This testimony by witness Robert -- by Rutten is to be found in page 5231 hearing of 7th of December, 2006, but this is also what Robert Franken testified: He could not remember any problems with the UNHCR. He only remembered after he read an excerpt of the NIOD report, 5D54. He only then remembered that he had tried to impose a control of the UNHCR convoy. But he could not remember that the said convoy had failed to enter Srebrenica precisely because of what he had done, because of what he had decided; 18th of October, 2006 hearing, transcript pages 2639/2640. We're now in June 1995. The Muslim forces have launched a generalised offensive on the Serb positions, including in Sarajevo, but the forces in Srebrenica and Zepa also contributed, as is shown by Exhibit 5D229. However, the UNHCR convoy bound for Srebrenica was allowed to pass through by the Serb authorities. It went through the VRS check-point, but it did not enter Srebrenica. In June 1995, the humanitarian situation was difficult everywhere. It was difficult in Srebrenica as well. But Robert Franken, the assistant commander of the DutchBat, decided, at the ABiH request, to impose control of the UNHCR convoy, which caused the convoy to depart, which caused the convoy not to supply the aid it had brought. Robert Franken forgot the UNHCR convoy. He also forgot that the DutchBat that he commanded in second would -- used to seek supplies from Bratunac. Of course there were restrictions, but they were limited in nature, and, above all, they had not been imposed in order to create living conditions that would be unbearable for the Muslim populations. They were the result of numerous abuses by the ABiH and by those who transported humanitarian aid. Nobody can rule out the possibility that restrictions, if any, were justified. Let me take the example quoted by the Prosecutor, the case of a truck transporting school supplies. This ban seems odd. Why should one ban school supplies? Very simply, because the request was made in June. In June, children are on holiday. However, the ABiH could make good use of copy books that were to be used initially by children. Everybody remembers the copy books used by the intercept operators. Just have a look at them. Look, for instance, at P2328. You will see that these were copy books used by children, but this time they had been used for military purposes by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like to add a few words regarding medical supplies. The Prosecutor claims that there was nobody left in Potocari when 5D1446, this report, was drafted. The report only supports the excerpt from 14 the NIOD report whose number 5D53 was inadvertently omitted from footnote 568 in our Defence Final Brief. Of course, there was still wounded people in Potocari on the 13th of July, 1995. They were evacuated only on the 18th of July, 1995. Even Robert Franken admitted that there were wounded left in the Potocari base after the population had been evacuated. Eelco [as interpreted] Koster testified, too, in his 92 ter statement that the wounded stayed in the DutchBat base. The UNMO report of 17th of July, 1995, P524, confirms that on the 17th of July, 1995, the wounded people were still in Potocari. Could we move to closed session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let me speak for a few moments about the evacuation of the wounded from Potocari. We have set out our arguments in paragraphs 343 to 349 of our brief. Let me just say that this evacuation had been requested by DutchBat. Robert Franken said so on the 16th of October, 2006, transcripts pages 2515, by MSF, and that on the 16th of July, General Nicolai was eagerly awaiting the authorisation to take to Potocari the convoy that was to evacuate the wounded; Exhibit P1191 and P2978. When the notifications bearing the name of General Miletic were sent, the evacuation of the wounded was the only possible solution. It is obvious that neither DutchBat nor MSF were going to stay in Potocari and that the wounded had to be evacuated. I doubt very much that the Prosecutor, who elsewhere alleged that there were no medical supplies in Potocari, seriously suggested that these notifications should not have been sent and that the evacuation of wounded -- of the wounded was not necessary. Let us now address the issue of the transmission of messages mentioned by the Prosecutor on the 2nd of September, P1237. The Defence does not challenge that General Miletic could have transmitted the message, and it is possible that this message was about the evacuation. However, the conversation in which General Miletic was mentioned does not allow any conclusion as to the knowledge General Miletic may have had of the very subject of the request made, and even less as to General Miletic's intention. The only conclusion this conversation allows is that General Miletic was not authorised to take a decision. What could General Miletic do, faced with such a situation? Was he supposed to turn down and refuse the message to be transmitted and, therefore, to block this evacuation that was requested by all international organisations in BiH, including the UNPROFOR? We do not think that document P260, which was transmitted at 17 hours on 18th of July, has any link with the conversation that took place at 21 hours on 17th of July, P1237. It is very unlikely -- it is improbable that Colonel Jankovic would have waited 24 hours to make his request. Furthermore, Exhibit P260 refers to the 18th of July events, and these events could not have been the topic of a conversation that was taking place the day before. Let me return briefly to the issue of humanitarian aid. The Prosecution case, that the Serbian authorities demanded responsibility -- reciprocity and made their conditional [as interpreted] of humanitarian aid to Muslims conditional on aid being provided to the Serbs, stands in contradiction to the case that the restrictions aimed at creating an unbearable situation for the Muslim population. If reciprocity had been the condition set by the Serbs, the restrictions that were in any way limited cannot be ascribed to the intent of creating unbearable conditions for the Muslims, but rather to the will to make sure that the Serbs had the best possible conditions. However, this case, even though it is to some extent favourable to the Defence, is incorrect. Reciprocity was requested one single time -- what is alleged by the Prosecutor in paragraph 226, footnote 513, namely, that fuel was authorised for the enclaves only if Serbs were to receive some as well, this allegation is incorrect. Further to Exhibit P2689, the fuel for Srebrenica was authorised unconditionally. When the Serb authorities asked humanitarian aid supply for the Serbs to allow the passage of a convoy, the convoy was not destined for the Muslim population. It was destined to supply the UNPROFOR. This was said on -- this happened on the 1st of July, 1995, P2554. In our closing brief, we mention problems linked with humanitarian aid in June 1995, problems that were not at all linked to Serb policy. In June 1995, the UNHCR had foreseen 1250 tonnes of humanitarian aid for Banja Luka. Exhibit P4145, page 19, shows that nothing reached its destination. When I say nothing arrived, nothing at all arrived. Faced with such a situation, once and only once did the Serb authorities request reciprocity, which did not in any way jeopardise supplies destined for the Muslim populations. The humanitarian aid convoys and the UNPROFOR convoys were different in every respect. They also had to undergo different procedures. This is an essential difference, because contrary to what the Prosecutor alleged, the coordination organ did give authorisations for humanitarian convoys. This was mentioned in paragraph 322 to 342 of our brief. Furthermore, the Prosecutor has original Main Staff documents regarding the convoys which were, incidentally, stipulated between the Prosecution and the Miletic Defence. This is Exhibit 5D1447. All these documents have to do with UNPROFOR convoys. If the procedure had been the same, we would have found, among these documents, documents related to humanitarian convoys. But I'm not interested in the confusion between humanitarian convoys and UNPROFOR convoys which pervades the entire Prosecutor's brief, but I'm interested in the confusion between the part of the brief regarding the alleged contribution of General Miletic to restrictions to the convoys, paragraphs 1679 to 1687, and the general part regarding restrictions to humanitarian aid, paragraphs 215 to 250. In paragraph 219 of their brief, the Prosecution described the procedure by which authorisations were given to UNPROFOR convoys. The Prosecutor acknowledged that General Miletic did not take any decisions. The Prosecution further acknowledged that General Miletic did not draft any notifications. Indeed, the Prosecutor acknowledged that the part played by General Miletic was to sign a notification and to send them to subordinate units. Although the Prosecutor acknowledged that General Miletic did not play any part in taking decisions or in determining the contents of notifications, in paragraph 1679 of their brief, despite the evidence in its totality and in contradiction to their own case as set out in paragraph 219, the Prosecutor alleged that General Miletic refused to grant passage for the convoys with school supplies, would have limited MSF personnel rotation, and would have specified a request for control. In the same paragraph, the Prosecutor alleged that General Miletic was involved in sending notifications on the 6th and the 10th of March, 1995, referring to unsigned copies of the notifications, P2522 and P2531. The original and signed versions of the notifications have been admitted into evidence; 5D1311 and 5D1312. These notifications were not signed by General Miletic. They were signed by Colonel Pandzic, who was not even a subordinate of General Miletic. There is no evidence that General Miletic ever saw the documents. Furthermore, the other notifications referred to by the Prosecutor in paragraph 1679 are all unsigned copies. Taking into account the fact that there are many notifications bearing the name, but not the signature of General Miletic, which emerges from the stipulations between the Defence and the Prosecutor, 5D1447, there is no conclusive evidence that the notification, the signed version of which was not available, were ever signed by General Miletic. One has also to say that the sending of the notifications did not contribute at all in the questions of humanitarian aid for as much as they had to. The notifications did not have, as a goal, to prevent the passage of the convoys, but to allow it. No convoy could pass the control point or check-point without having been announced by a notification of the Main Staff. Even when a notification contained the information concerning an unauthorised convoy, it had no impact on the passage of the convoy, because until the notification authorising convoy and supplies reached the check-point, the convoy could not go through, could not pass. And announcing the convoys and the control of the same was quite licit and conformed to the Geneva Conventions. Let's just see what General Miletic knew about the humanitarian aid. When General Milovanovic was not at the Main Staff, the name of General Miletic was on the notification. He signed a certain number of them, but he never took the authority of the general for substantial matters linked to humanitarian aid, so authority of General Milovanovic were taken over by other officers of the Main Staff, including by General Mladic. General Miletic did not take part in the meetings of UNPROFOR. He did not take part to the meetings of the international organisations. He was not a superior to Colonel Djurdjic, who was in charge of the convoys. He did not give him any instructions. General Miletic was not a member of the inner circle of the Main Staff and took no decisions. Besides, in the section of his brief concerning the Serbian policies of the political and military authorities concerning humanitarian aid, paragraph 246 to 250, the Prosecutor did not mention General Miletic, thereby acknowledging implicitly that General Miletic had no role in the devising of this policy. General Miletic had no role in the follow-up of the convoys because the reports concerning them were not sent to his administration, but to the Intelligence Administration; P260. Precisely in this context, one should interpret notification of the 29th of June, 1995, P2551, mentioned by the Prosecution at paragraph 1683. Although this notification contains a note concerning specific instructions sent to Momir Nikolic, there is no evidence that General Miletic knew about this instruction which had certainly been -- knew anything about the content of this instruction which certainly had to be sent to Momir Nikolic directly through the -- from the Intelligence Sector and Security Sector. Also, the reports concerning the convoys were directly sent and personally sent to General Mladic, as was the case for the 23rd of June, 1995; P2496. General Miletic knew nothing, in particular, about questions concerning humanitarian aid. What General Miletic knew was that the notification had to be sent in order to enable the passage of a convoy. No officer would have refused to sign and send such a notification. This notification question shows no personal intention of General Miletic. Indeed, the only document and the only evidence which can inform us of the position of General Miletic about the passage of convoys is the intercepted conversation of the 24th of July, 1995, P1327, concerning the problems linked to the passage of convoy to Gorazde described also in a document from the Drina Corps, P3035. This conversation shows that General Miletic, when he knew about the problems concerning the passage of a convoy, considered that such problems had to be solved. Let us now speak about Directive number 7. This is the centre of the case against General Miletic. We agree with the Prosecution that during the drafting of this directive, the complete method was used. Within the framework of this complete method, which had been decided by the commander and the commander only, General Miletic was able only to do his own part of the work. We agree with the Prosecution that the different elements of the directive were transmitted to General Miletic by the different sectors of the Main Staff and that General Miletic then compiled them to make a single document. While acknowledging that Directive number 7 was drafted by an application of the complete method, the Prosecution implicitly acknowledged that General Miletic was not the author of the contents of this directive. The only fact of having taken part in the drafting of Directive number 7 does not mean that General Mladic contributed to the joint criminal enterprise -- General Miletic, as alleged in the indictment. The Prosecutor could speak of a contribution of General Miletic if he had proved that General Miletic had drafted the offending parts of the directive or that he had accepted them, adhered to them. Yet the Prosecution did not prove any such thing. The Prosecutor acknowledged in paragraph 1680 that General Miletic had seen the document of the Drina Corps in which the commander of the Drina Corps proposed some solutions for the elimination of the enclaves. Beyond the fact that this proposal shows very well that the corps commanders were making proposals to the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, this tells us nothing about the position of General Miletic. He saw it, but there is no evidence that he was in agreement with it or that this proposal had been included in the draft directive drafted by General Miletic. Besides, the Prosecution alleges that General Miletic compiled the part of the directive concerning the tasks of the units on the basis of the proposals of organs charged with a different army corps; paragraph 1663. General Miletic compiled the whole project of the directive on the basis of the elements obtained from the different organs, as the Prosecutor acknowledges in paragraph 141. On the basis of the evidence in the case file, it is impossible to say who supplied him with the proposal for the part concerning the tasks of the units. The text drafted by General Miletic was the draft of the directive. The text of this draft is not known, and there is no evidence which enables us to conclude that this draft contained the offending passages of Directive number 7. In his brief, at paragraph 142, the Prosecution admits that President Karadzic could amend the draft directive drafted by General Miletic. This also means that President Karadzic could add the incriminated passages and in the offending passages. Contrarily-wise to what the Prosecutor alleges, the directive was not issued under the name of General Miletic. Also, it was not sent to the corps as a document from the general who at the time was Colonel Miletic, but as a document from president and supreme command, Radovan Karadzic. The Prosecutor's allegation according to which General Miletic should have known every word contained in these directives before signing his name on the text is absurd. The name of General Miletic on the text of this directive means he prepared the draft directive and certainly doesn't mean that he approved the final text of the directive. The final text belonged to President Karadzic, who had the single and exclusive authority to approve it, which he did by putting his signature on it. General Miletic could have known and should have known every word of the draft directive that was sent to President Karadzic for signing, but as for the final text of the directive, General Miletic could not know it before it was transmitted to him, yet there is no evidence in the case file to show that General Miletic would have seen the final text of Directive 7 before he started working on the draft Directive 7/1. In his closing argument on the 2nd of September, 2009, the Prosecution stated that there was no evidence which would have confirmed that General Miletic might have not taken part in the finalisation of Directive 7. Contrarily-wise to -- in this business, there is no evidence that General Miletic would have taken part in the finalisation of the directive. General Simic, indeed, spoke about the finalisation, but it was a finalisation of the draft, because all the processes which General Simic has described takes place before the draft was sent for his signature on the 19th of November, 2008; page 28511. This statement made by General Simic helps in no way the Prosecution in its efforts to show that General Miletic would have taken part in the finalisation of the directive after the changes brought by -- after the changes President Karadzic may have brought to it. The onus of proving this remains with the Prosecution, and the Prosecution has to prove each and every one of his allegations beyond any reasonable doubt. The Defence has not got the same onus. It suffices for it to adduce evidence showing that another possibility is reasonable. Evidence, of course, which is circumstantial, as they may be, show, in fact, that General Miletic did not take part in the finalisation of the final text of Directive 7. The Defence agrees with the Prosecution that General Miletic should have told General Milovanovic, as he had seen the offending parts of the text or the directive. We consider that there exists at least a reasonable possibility that General Miletic did so. The directive bears the date of the 8th of March, 1995, while it was sent to the corps only on the 17th of March, 1995. The agenda of President Karadzic, Exhibit 5D1322, shows that on the eve of the transmission of the directive to the corps, General Milovanovic had a meeting with President Karadzic. The only reasonable explanation of this meeting, which lasted four hours and which took place on the 16th of March, 1995, would have been about a discussion on Directive number 7. The Prosecution stated also that General Miletic could have done something else and could have acted contrarily if he had not been in agreement with the directive. We entirely agree. General Miletic could have refused to send the directive to the corps. The Prosecution will certainly tell you that there is no evidence that General Miletic refused to transmit Directive 7 to the corps, and in a certain sense he is right, but only partially, because if there is no evidence that General Miletic refused to transmit the directive to the corps, we do have the proof that he did not further it or forward it; P5 and 5D971 confirms this. The only thing which is proven in this case concerning the final version of Directive 7 is that it was transmitted to the subordinate units by General Milovanovic. Since General Miletic did not transmit Directive 7 to the corps, there are only two options concerning the knowledge he may have had of the final text. Either General Milovanovic transmitted the final version of Directive 7 to the corps as soon as he was back from the meeting with President Karadzic without telling General Miletic, or General Miletic was unwilling to forward it. The Prosecution adduced no evidence which might have supported his case according to which General Miletic adhered to the final version of Directive 7. The evidence, circumstantial evidence, leads to the conclusion of the opposite, which is General Miletic was not in agreement with the directive. This is a possible and reasonable conclusion, which explains the meeting which General Milovanovic had with President Karadzic on the 16th of March, 1995. And the belated or delayed transmission of the directive, practically ten days after the date indicated on the text of the directive, and the fact that General Miletic did not forward it. General Miletic did take part in the drafting of Directive 7/1, and his role in the drafting of Directive 7.1, it was identical to his role in the drafting of Directive 7. Such participation cannot be interpreted as his adhering to the text of Directive number 7, since the text of Directive 7/1 does not contain the offending passages contained in Directive 7. The very existence of Directive 7/1 asks us the question of why this directive was drafted. Before Directive 7, only Directive 6 came from President Karadzic. This is Exhibit P3919. Following Directive 6, the Main Staff did not draft Directive 6.1. On the contrary, when President Karadzic considered that the text of Directive 6 had to be changed, he did so by a document which he signed, himself, 5D964. Directive number 7 indicated the tasks to be performed by the corps, and it was transmitted to the corps. There is no military reason for the Main Staff to embark in the drafting of Directive 7/1 immediately after the transmission of Directive 7. This was not necessary for the performance of Operation Spreca, since General Milovanovic had sent the order to the corps for this operation; 5D972. Operation Sadejstvo planned at the Main Staff did not require either to dispatch Directive 7/1 at the end of March 1995, since all the details of this operation were sent to the corps only towards the end of the month of April; P4202. One of the possible explanations, and a perfectly reasonable explanation, for issuing Directive 7/1 was precisely that this directive, that is, Directive 7/1, was made to replace Directive 7 in the subordinated units. Almost in every sentence related to General Miletic, the Prosecutor quotes General Milovanovic, although he does not consider him credible. He completely ignored his explanation about Directive 7.7 -- Directive 7. It is indicative, though, that precisely General Milovanovic, who denied any part in the drafting of these two directives, and who proclaimed that he had no knowledge of their existence, declared that General Mladic was risking to be arraigned in front of a martial court because he had omitted parts of Directive 7 in the documents which he subsequently drafted. There is no doubt that General Milovanovic was more specifically speaking of directive 7. The part taken by General Miletic in the drafting of Directive 7 and 7/1 cannot be interpreted as his adhering to the offending parts of Directive 7. The existence of his name on Directive 7 and 7/1, to the utmost, allows to conclude that when Directive 7/1 was drafted, he had cognizance of the final text of Directive 7. Such knowledge does not mean that he adhered to the offending parts of Directive 7. Subsequent events show that General Miletic had no significant part in the events concerning Srebrenica and Zepa, that he was absent during the military operation at Srebrenica, that he had no sufficient knowledge concerning the events on the ground, and that his acts and behaviour do not allow an inference about his intention to contribute to forced transfer. The Prosecution stated that Directive 7 concerned the inception of the attack, yet during the hearing of the 10th of December, 2008, page 24489-24490, the Prosecution declared that the Army of Republika Srpska did not change its behaviour after Directive number 7 and that this behaviour was the same as at the beginning of the war. We agree with the Prosecution that no change can be noted in the behaviour of the Army of the Republika Srpska after the issuance of Directive number 7, but in that case it is difficult to understand how Directive 7 represented the beginning of the attack. Besides, there is no evidence that a systematic attack or generalised attack against the population -- civil population would have started in March 1995. Be that as it is, General Milovanovic was present at the general headquarters of the Main Staff for a long period following the issuance of Directive 7. No evidence allows to conclude that General Miletic knew about the incidents linked to the bombing, or snipers, or other activities around Srebrenica and Zepa, inasmuch as such activities are established. The only bombing which is reported to the Main Staff was that which took place on the 25th of May, 1995, yet General Milovanovic was there; Exhibit 3D-5D1161. It is absurd to establish a link between the training programme of snipers and the possible use, in an illegal way, of snipers. The body was one in charge of operational matters and training, was in charge of organising and planning training, this organ could not determine the content of the training, since every training requires specific knowledge and since the content of this training was precisely determined by specialised organs for different subjects. Anyway, the programme mentioned by the Prosecutor was not meant to -- was not meant for an illegal use of snipers, but precisely for the correct use of snipers. Snipers are not a forbidden weapon, and the existence of a training programme has no specific meaning. Finally, it remains unknown when the programme was drafted and when it was transmitted to the corps. The programme which we have in the case file was transmitted to the 5th Corps, which in 1995 didn't even exist. The Prosecutor alleges that the acts and decisions of General Miletic were crucial to defeat, militarily, the Muslim forces and to transfer the population of Srebrenica and Zepa. I have already said that General Miletic was not even in a position to make decisions, but I shall not belabour this point. Rather, I would like to underscore the confusion created between acts which are destined to defeat, militarily, Muslim forces and those which were destined to forcibly transfer the population. Military defeat of the enemy, which for the Army of Republika Srpska, were the Muslim forces, is a natural and legitimate objective for any army in an armed conflict. On the other hand, the forcible transfer of population is a forbidden act and is a crime. In order to prove forcible transfer and, in particular, the intention of the accused, the Prosecutor should have made a clear distinction between the military objectives and the criminal objectives. Indeed, when an act may reasonably be interpreted as being destined or meant to achieve a legitimate military objective, the Prosecutor cannot attribute to him a criminal intention. This intention can only be inferred from facts which cannot reasonably be explained by a legitimate military objective and which allow no other conclusion than what was meant for the transfer of the Muslim population. It is difficult, in a conflict like this one, indeed, to distinguish between the facts connected with a military attack and the facts connected with criminal acts, yet the Prosecutor has the duty to do so. In the present case, the Prosecutor stated several times that the separation of the enclaves was a legitimate military goal; in particular, in the preliminary statement of 21st August 2006, page 398. He cannot now, for the purpose of his own closing argument, make a confusion between this legitimate part of the attack and a criminal objective. We agree with the Prosecutor when he states that the intent will determine the legitimacy of an act and that a legitimate act, accomplished with a criminal intent, may become criminal. Yet if intent confers a criminal character to an act which, without such intent, would have been legitimate, this act will only be criminal in respect to those who acted with a criminal intention, but will be legitimate for those who did not act with such intention. For General Miletic, the Prosecutor did not prove that he acted with a criminal intention. The Prosecutor alleges that General Miletic followed the Drina Corps activities and forwarded the information he obtained to General Mladic and President Karadzic. The Prosecutor alleged that precisely this information would have enabled General Mladic and President Karadzic to make the decisions and to apply the policy of forced -- forcible transfer. First of all, the Prosecution did not prove that President Karadzic took decisions on the basis of the reports sent by General Miletic. The Prosecutor did not even indicate which would have been the information which would contribute to the decisions of President Karadzic. We have indicated in paragraph 492 of our brief the sources from which President Karadzic obtained the information. There are many of them. The decisions concerning Srebrenica and Zepa were certainly not made on the basis of the reports sent by General Miletic, daily reports. As for General Mladic, he had no need of the reports of General Miletic. He received direct information from the commanders of the corps which were subordinated to him. The evidence in this case shows that the civilian authorities informed President Karadzic. This evidence shows that a delegation of Skelani was to meet President Karadzic after the action at Zeleni Jadar in order to find a solution to put an end to this action which the civilian authorities considered as incomplete. This is Exhibits 5D1374. The evidence in this case also shows that President Karadzic sometimes had much more information than the Main Staff. Intercept of 16 July 1995 shows that precisely President Karadzic informed the Main Staff of the opening of the Zvornik corridor. In the daily reports of the Main Staff, we have a description of the military situation on the ground in all the territory of the Republika Srpska. Their goal was no other than to inform President Karadzic and the commander of the corps of this military situation, and no other interpretation may reasonably be attributed to such reports. Neither the follow-up of the military situation which General Miletic could not keep track of, except on the basis of the reports he received, nor the transmission of this information, could reasonably be interpreted as contributing to the criminal enterprise as alleged. None of these acts is illicit. These acts constitute the regular and daily duties of General Miletic. On the 2nd September, 2009, the Prosecutor started his final speech by the duty for officers to complete their duty, the duty of the officer in charge of operational matters is to draft and transmit reports. These acts are precisely what the general did. These acts are precisely what the general did. These acts are the acts of any officer in charge of operational matters and what any officer would have done. No officer in charge of operational matters would have done otherwise. No criminal intention may be inferred from the report sent by General Miletic because for these reports there is another logical and reasonable explanation which, by the way, is the only reasonable explanation about it. General Miletic was doing his job. This job was legal, licit, regular, and necessary for the furthering of legitimate and justified military activities. He did so without any criminal intent.
